Our method for the SHROOM-Visions 2026 Shared Task explores a parameter-efficient solution by fine-tuning a lightweight token-level classification head on the frozen weights of the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct vision-language model. We utilized category-specific thresholds calculated based on validation character-level IoU and designed a span merging post-processing step to facilitate span localization with fewer fragmented predictions. We also establish a possible connection between the annotator agreement and the operating thresholds. Our analysis suggests that, within our experimental setup, hallucination categories that had higher inter-annotator agreement tended to have higher optimal decision thresholds whereas categories with lower agreement tended to have lower optimal decision thresholds. Our parameter-efficient method achieved ranks 18th, 16th, 16th, and 15th place on the English, French, Italian, and Chinese tracks, respectively, showing promising performance for multilingual fine-grained hallucination detection.

paper.title: SpanCalib-VLM: Calibrated Hallucination Span Detection in Vision-Language Models
paper.abstract: Detecting hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) requires both accurate span localization and well-calibrated confidence scores. Fine-tuned generative VLMs excel at identifying hallucinated text spans but suffer from overconfidence and high inference latency. Discriminative sequence taggers offer deterministic speed and superior calibration but exhibit conservative span recall. We present SpanCalib-VLM, a hybrid dual-system for the SHROOM-Visions Shared Task that combines a multimodal sequence tagger, consisting of XLM-RoBERTa-Large fused with a SigLIP vision encoder via cross-attention, with our fine-tuned generative VLM (Qwen3.5-4B-SHROOM-SFT). Through a Union-Calibrated Fusion strategy, candidate spans from the generative model are re-scored with calibrated probabilities from the sequence tagger. On the SHROOM-Visions English validation split, our ensemble achieves a Pearson calibration correlation of 0.41 and an overall IoU of 0.39 (with a clean-response IoU of 0.91 and overall detection accuracy of 70.7%). On the official blind test set, SpanCalib-VLM achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.32 and an IoU of 0.25 on English, substantially outperforming the shared task baseline (0.15 on both metrics) and demonstrating consistent gains across all four languages. We make our model weights and code publicly available.

paper.title: Team hccl-jy at SHROOM-Visions: Confidence Signals from an Unmodified VLM Verifier
paper.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can describe details an image does not support. Detecting such hallucinations requires locating the unsupported text rather than flagging whole responses. The SHROOM-Visions shared task asks systems to localize these spans, classify their error type, and assign character-level probabilities. This paper describes the hccl-jy English-track submission. We ask whether confidence from a pretrained VLM verifier can support this task without fine-tuning, and whether candidate-level gains survive extraction and aggregation. The system runs an unmodified Qwen2.5-VL verifier over spaCy candidates with exact character offsets. An aggregation model fitted on held-out calibration data converts candidate judgments into output spans. We compare verbalized confidence, verdict-token probability, and five-draw consistency against annotator agreement, calibration error, and the official metrics. Verdict-token probability separates high-agreement candidates from low-agreement ones more reliably at 32B than at 7B. Averaging repeated judgments improves this ranking further but does not improve the official score. Error analysis shows that the initial score comes mostly from correct empty predictions and that error typing is weak for invented content. Revising only the aggregation over cached judgments raises Cor on development and test data. The findings support evaluating confidence discrimination, calibration, and end-to-end performance as separate targets.

paper.title: Sckwoky at SHROOM-Visions: Character-Level Hallucination-Span Detection in Image-Conditioned VLMs via Dual-Prompted LoRA Decoders
paper.abstract: We present our system for the SHROOM-visions 2026 shared task on character-level hallucination span detection in image-conditioned vision-language model (VLM) responses, evaluated across English, French, Italian, and Chinese. The detector is built on a frozen Gemma-4-12B-it backbone with trainable LoRA adapters (\sim10.7M parameters). Because the backbone is a causal decoder, hidden states read from a single copy of an answer cannot attend to subsequent tokens; we therefore repeat the candidate answer within one prompt and extract features from its second occurrence, giving every position approximate bidirectional context in a single non-autoregressive pass. A character-level locator combines intermediate hidden states to predict hallucination probabilities, BIO boundaries, and a response-level abstention score, while separate language-specific classifiers assign one of five hallucination types to each predicted span. On the closed test set, our system reaches a macro-averaged character IoU of 0.4400, roughly doubling the official baseline (0.1850), and ranks 5th–6th on IoU across the four languages. In deployments where the same Gemma-4-12B-it model also generates answers, its base weights can be reused, making the approach practical for local question-answering systems that cannot run a separate verifier.

paper.title: Team champ at SHROOM-Visions: Transferring Fine-Grained Hallucination Detection with Hidden-State Probes and Backbone Adaptation
paper.abstract: We describe a multilingual, character-level hallucination detection system for vision-language models combining multi-layer hidden states, text-to-vision LoRA transfer, multitask learning, and language-specific span emission. Our submission achieved a validation Character AUPRC of 0.5530 and an average test Cor/Cor+lbl of 0.5243/0.4174. A controlled post-submission factorial analysis improved validation Character AUPRC to 0.5595. Team champ placed third in French, fourth in Italian and Chinese, and fifth in English.

paper.title: TÜRKSAT at SHROOM-Visions: Crowd-Emulating Judge Ensembles for Multilingual Hallucination Span Detection in Vision-Language Models
paper.abstract: We describe our submission to SHROOM-Visions 2026, the shared task on generator-agnostic, character-level hallucination span detection and typing in vision-language model outputs across English, French, Italian, and Chinese. Rather than training a detector, we use a crowd-emulating judge ensemble: one instruction-tuned multimodal model, sampled at several temperatures and with several prompt variants, independently re-inspects each image, prompt, and response and proposes typed hallucination spans. Character-level vote fractions form soft probabilities that emulate the multi-annotator gold labels, while a cross-validated threshold per language produces hard spans. The black-box system requires no parameter updates and relies on guideline-derived prompt rules and language-specific few-shot examples. On the official closed test set, it ranks first for all English metrics and for Italian IoU, and second for every remaining language-metric combination. Official scores range from 0.4336 to 0.4845 for Cor+Lbl, 0.5474 to 0.5814 for Cor, and 0.4865 to 0.5240 for IoU. On held-out training folds, IoU is 0.32 to 0.39 on non-empty items. Ablations identify prompt design and few-shot conditioning as decisive, while an added adjudication stage does not improve performance. Vote fractions track annotator agreement but remain globally over-confident (ECE 0.08 to 0.12), motivating per-language thresholding.

paper.title: HalluVision at SHROOM-Vision: Hallucination Span Detection with a Classifier over a Vision-Language Backbone
paper.abstract: We present our system for the SHROOM-Visions 2026 shared task on fine-grained hallucination detection in vision-language model (VLM) outputs. Our approach uses three token-level internal signals from Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct: hidden representations, the change in token confidence when the image is removed, and predictive uncertainty. A lightweight classifier combines these signals to predict hallucinated spans and their confidence, while LoRA enables parameter-efficient adaptation of the VLM backbone. Our submission achieves IoU scores of 0.36–0.42 and Spearman correlations of 0.41–0.46 on English, French, and Italian, ranking 10th in both French and Italian. We additionally analyze continued-training experiments that improved our local validation scores but consistently degraded official test performance. Our analysis attributes this discrepancy primarily to threshold tuning on a small validation split, which was only partially mitigated by subsequent adjustments. Increasing the backbone size from 3B to 7B parameters did not resolve the issue. These findings highlight the sensitivity of hallucination detection systems to validation size and decision-threshold selection.
